title: Not alone in it
hook: Christians see in the cross a God who suffers with humanity

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Gethsemane, the garden where Jesus asked for the cup to pass. Your line was not as I will, but as thou wilt.
screen: `NOT AS I WILL, BUT AS THOU WILT.`

segments.voice: The garden prayer asked for the cup to pass. In Matthew's telling, it doesn't. Within hours there is an arrest, a trial before the high priest, a night of denials, and then a place called Golgotha. Christian teaching reads the cross in more than one way: some readings ask what it paid for, or what it won. Today's asks something quieter. Who is on that cross, and which side of the pain is he standing on? Watching it from above, or inside it?
screen: `THE CUP DOES NOT PASS.` → `A PLACE CALLED GOLGOTHA.` → `WHICH SIDE OF THE PAIN?`

segments.voice: First, a name. In its first chapter, Matthew's Gospel gives a child the name Emmanuel, and translates it for its readers: "God with us." Not above us, not watching us. With. Second, the cross. Christians read the crucifixion through that name. In their telling, the one hanging there is no stranger to pain, watching from far off. He is inside it: betrayed by a friend, deserted, beaten, mocked. Near the end, Matthew records him crying out the opening line of a psalm: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" That's the King James wording. Even feeling abandoned, in this reading, is a place he has been. Third, a letter. The Letter to the Hebrews says: "For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities." A double negative, almost shy. It means he can be touched. He knows weakness from the inside. Fourth, how churches say it. Some theologians speak of God himself suffering on the cross. Others hold that the divine nature cannot suffer, and that the Son suffered truly in his human nature. Both keep hold of the same thing: on the cross, Christians say, God came into the worst of human pain, not only above it. The cup is not taken away. In this reading, it is drunk by someone inside suffering, so that nobody in it is alone.
screen: `EMMANUEL: GOD WITH US.` · `INSIDE THE PAIN, NOT WATCHING IT.` · `TOUCHED WITH THE FEELING.` · `CHURCHES SAY IT DIFFERENT WAYS.` · then, large: `NOT ALONE IN IT.`

segments.voice: Picture someone who is suffering right now: a friend, a parent, a neighbor, someone in the news. Breathing in, say their name silently; breathing out, say: not alone, and if the mind starts drafting advice, let the draft go and come back to the name. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer.
Emmanuel, the name Matthew gives Jesus, meaning God with us, inside suffering and not only above it. Today's word.
Your line: he can be touched. No advice needed, only company. That's day seven hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Christians meditate on the cross, especially in Holy Week and on Good Friday, as the place where God shares human suffering, and visit the sick and grieving as a work of mercy.

fork.setup: you're reading Hebrews: "we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities." what is the double negative saying?
options: he is kept far from human weakness.
he can be touched; he knows weakness from the inside.
fork.reveal: "not... cannot" means he can. Christians read it as a God who knows suffering from the inside, not from a distance.

what a scholar hears: Emmanuel in Matthew 1:23, the cry of Psalm 22 in Matthew 27:46, Hebrews 4:15, and an old debate over whether the divine nature can suffer.

chat.says: Why do Christians call Jesus Emmanuel?
options: It means God with us: in their reading, God came inside human pain.
It means God watches over us from a safe distance, above the pain.
It was simply his family name, the one people used in his town.
chat.meaning: Matthew translates Emmanuel as God with us. Christians read the cross through that name: God inside suffering, not only above it.

Emmanuel.meaning: a name Matthew translates as God with us

Golgotha.meaning: the place where Jesus was crucified

Letter to the Hebrews.meaning: a New Testament letter that speaks of Christ as high priest

King James.meaning: an old, much-loved English translation of the Bible

notes: The two ways of speaking about Christ's suffering (God suffering on the cross vs. the divine nature being impassible and the Son suffering in his human nature) are given without ranking or attribution to named churches; a Keeper may want named examples or a softer summary.
'With the older creeds' refers loosely to the classical (Chalcedonian) tradition of divine impassibility; confirm the phrasing is fair.
Matthew 27:46 is the opening of Psalm 22; the script says 'the opening line of a psalm' without numbering it in voice. Confirm.
Practice and carry follow the outline (keep company with someone suffering).
